title: The Spirit Comes: Witness Begins
lesson: Luke opens Acts with Jesus’ forty days of appearances and a clear commission: wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit, then be witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. After the ascension, about 120 believers devote themselves to prayer, and Matthias is chosen to replace Judas among the apostles.

At Pentecost the Spirit fills the disciples with wind-and-fire power. Peter proclaims the crucified and risen Christ; about three thousand repent, are baptized, and devote themselves to teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer. The church’s life is Word, community, worship, and prayer—and the Lord adds to their number daily.

At the Beautiful Gate, Peter heals a man lame from birth in Jesus’ name and calls Israel to repent. Arrested for preaching the resurrection, Peter tells the Sanhedrin that salvation is found in no other name. The church prays for boldness; the place is shaken, they speak God’s word boldly, and share so that none among them are needy.

featuredVerse.text: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

questions.prompt: According to Acts 1:8, where would the apostles be witnesses?
choices: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and the ends of the earth
questions.explanation: Acts 1:8 maps the mission: Jerusalem → Judea/Samaria → the ends of the earth.

questions.prompt: What filled the house at Pentecost?
choices: A sound like a violent wind
questions.explanation: A sound like the blowing of a violent wind came from heaven and filled the house (Acts 2:2).

questions.prompt: About how many were added to the church on Pentecost?
questions.explanation: About three thousand accepted the message and were baptized (Acts 2:41).

questions.prompt: In whose name did Peter heal the lame man at the temple gate?
questions.explanation: “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk” (Acts 3:6).

questions.prompt: Peter told the Sanhedrin that salvation is found:
choices: In no one else but Jesus
questions.explanation: Salvation is found in no one else; there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12).

questions.prompt: After release, the believers prayed especially for:
questions.explanation: They asked God to enable them to speak His word with great boldness (Acts 4:29–31).

title: Integrity, Stephen, and a Spreading Gospel
lesson: Ananias and Sapphira’s lie about their gift brings sudden judgment and holy fear. The apostles heal many, are imprisoned, freed by an angel, and tell the council, “We must obey God rather than human beings.” Gamaliel warns that if the movement is of God it cannot be stopped; the apostles rejoice to suffer for the Name and keep teaching.

Seven Spirit-filled servants—including Stephen and Philip—are chosen so widows are cared for and the Word keeps spreading. Stephen’s bold retelling of Israel’s story ends with a vision of Jesus at God’s right hand. He is stoned, praying forgiveness for his killers, as Saul looks on.

Persecution scatters believers who preach wherever they go. Philip brings joy to Samaria; Simon learns God’s gift cannot be bought. On a desert road Philip explains Isaiah 53 to an Ethiopian official, baptizes him, and the gospel crosses new borders.

featuredVerse.text: Peter and the other apostles replied: “We must obey God rather than human beings!”

questions.prompt: What was Ananias and Sapphira’s main sin?
choices: Lying to the Holy Spirit about their gift
questions.explanation: They kept back part of the money and lied to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:1–4, 9).

questions.prompt: What principle did Peter state before the Sanhedrin?
choices: We must obey God rather than people
questions.explanation: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29).

questions.prompt: Why were seven men chosen in Acts 6?
questions.explanation: Widows were overlooked in the daily distribution; seven were chosen to wait on tables (Acts 6:1–6).

questions.prompt: What did Stephen see as he was dying?
choices: Jesus standing at God’s right hand
questions.explanation: He saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at God’s right hand (Acts 7:55–56).

questions.prompt: What happened when persecution scattered the church?
choices: They preached the word wherever they went
questions.explanation: Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went (Acts 8:4).

questions.prompt: After Philip explained Isaiah, the Ethiopian:
questions.explanation: “Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?” (Acts 8:36–38).

title: Saul Converted; Gentiles Welcomed; Prayer Answered
lesson: On the Damascus road Jesus stops Saul: “Why do you persecute me?” Blinded, then healed through obedient Ananias, Saul is baptized and immediately preaches that Jesus is the Son of God. Barnabas later vouches for him in Jerusalem. Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha; many turn to the Lord.

Cornelius the Gentile centurion and Peter both receive visions. Peter learns not to call impure what God has made clean, preaches peace through Jesus—Lord of all—and the Spirit falls on the household while he is still speaking. They are baptized. God shows no favoritism.

In Antioch disciples are first called Christians; the church sends famine relief. Herod kills James and imprisons Peter, but the church prays earnestly and an angel leads Peter out. Herod dies after accepting worship; the word of God continues to spread and flourish.

featuredVerse.text: Then Peter began to speak: “I now realize how true it is that God does not show favoritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears him and does what is right.”

questions.prompt: By persecuting believers, Jesus said Saul was:
questions.explanation: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4–5).

questions.prompt: What lesson did Peter’s vision teach?
choices: Do not call impure what God has made clean
questions.explanation: “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15).

questions.prompt: When did the Spirit fall on Cornelius’s household?
questions.explanation: While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard (Acts 10:44).

questions.prompt: Where were believers first called Christians?
questions.explanation: The disciples were called Christians first at Antioch (Acts 11:26).

questions.prompt: What was the church doing while Peter was in prison?
questions.explanation: The church was earnestly praying to God for him (Acts 12:5).

questions.prompt: After Herod’s death, Luke notes that:
choices: The word of God continued to spread
questions.explanation: But the word of God continued to spread and flourish (Acts 12:24).

title: Sent Out: Mission, Council, and Macedonia
lesson: While Antioch worships and fasts, the Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul. On Cyprus the proconsul believes; in Pisidian Antioch Paul proclaims forgiveness through the risen Jesus and turns to the Gentiles as a light to the nations. Joy and the Holy Spirit mark the disciples even amid opposition.

In Lystra Paul is nearly worshiped, then stoned—yet he returns to strengthen believers: we must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom. The Jerusalem council settles that Gentiles are saved by grace through the Lord Jesus, not by circumcision’s yoke. Antioch rejoices at the encouraging letter.

A Macedonian vision leads the team to Philippi. The Lord opens Lydia’s heart; Paul and Silas sing hymns in jail at midnight; the jailer believes—“Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved”—and his household is baptized. The gospel reaches a merchant, a slave girl, and a jailer alike.

featuredVerse.text: They replied, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.”

questions.prompt: How were Barnabas and Saul set apart for mission?
choices: By the Holy Spirit during worship and fasting
questions.explanation: While they were worshiping and fasting, the Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul” (Acts 13:2–3).

questions.prompt: What did Paul and Barnabas teach about entering the kingdom?
choices: We must go through many hardships
questions.explanation: We must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22).

questions.prompt: Peter’s conclusion at the Jerusalem council was that we are saved:
choices: Through the grace of the Lord Jesus
questions.explanation: Through the grace of our Lord Jesus we are saved, just as they are (Acts 15:11).

questions.prompt: How did the missionaries decide to go to Macedonia?
choices: A vision of a Macedonian man
questions.explanation: Paul saw a man of Macedonia begging, “Come over… and help us” (Acts 16:9–10).

questions.prompt: What did the Lord do for Lydia as she listened?
questions.explanation: The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message (Acts 16:14).

questions.prompt: What did Paul tell the jailer he must do to be saved?
questions.explanation: Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household (Acts 16:31).

title: Cities, Idols, and Shepherds of the Flock
lesson: In Thessalonica Paul reasons from Scripture that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Bereans examine the Scriptures daily. In Athens Paul proclaims the unknown God as Creator who calls all people everywhere to repent and will judge the world by the Man He raised from the dead.

In Corinth the Lord tells Paul not to fear—He has many people there. Paul stays eighteen months; Priscilla and Aquila later help Apollos know the way more accurately. In Ephesus the Spirit is given, sorcery scrolls are burned, and a riot over Artemis’s trade shows how the gospel threatens idols and markets.

At Miletus Paul charges the Ephesian elders: keep watch over yourselves and all the flock; wolves will come. He commits them to God and the word of His grace and recalls Jesus’ words: it is more blessed to give than to receive.

featuredVerse.text: Keep watch over yourselves and all the flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which he bought with his own blood.

questions.prompt: What made the Bereans noble?
questions.explanation: They examined the Scriptures every day to see if what Paul said was true (Acts 17:11).

questions.prompt: In Athens Paul said God now commands all people to:
questions.explanation: God commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30–31).

questions.prompt: In Corinth the Lord told Paul in a vision:
choices: Do not be afraid—I have many people in this city
questions.explanation: Do not be afraid; keep on speaking… I have many people in this city (Acts 18:9–10).

questions.prompt: What did former sorcerers in Ephesus do?
questions.explanation: They brought their scrolls together and burned them publicly (Acts 19:19).

questions.prompt: Paul charged the Ephesian elders to watch over:
questions.explanation: Keep watch over yourselves and all the flock… Be shepherds of the church of God (Acts 20:28).

questions.prompt: Which saying of Jesus did Paul recall about giving?
choices: It is more blessed to give than to receive
questions.explanation: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

title: Bound for Jesus’ Name: Arrest and Trials
lesson: Warned of chains, Paul still goes to Jerusalem, ready even to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. A temple riot erupts over rumors he defiled the holy place. On the steps he tells his Damascus story; mention of the Gentiles enrages the crowd. His Roman citizenship stops an unlawful flogging.

Before the Sanhedrin Paul stands on the hope of the resurrection, dividing Pharisees and Sadducees. That night the Lord stands near him: take courage—you must also testify in Rome. A plot of more than forty men is exposed by Paul’s nephew; soldiers escort him to Felix in Caesarea.

Before Felix, Paul worships the God of the ancestors, hopes in the resurrection, and speaks of righteousness, self-control, and judgment. Felix delays, hoping for a bribe, and leaves Paul imprisoned for two years—yet the Lord’s word about Rome still stands.

featuredVerse.text: The following night the Lord stood near Paul and said, “Take courage! As you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome.”

questions.prompt: How did Paul respond to warnings about suffering in Jerusalem?
choices: He said he was ready to be bound or die for Jesus’ name
questions.explanation: He was ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts 21:13).

questions.prompt: What especially angered the Jerusalem crowd in Paul’s defense?
questions.explanation: They listened until he said he was sent to the Gentiles (Acts 22:21–22).

questions.prompt: What hope did Paul highlight that split the council?
questions.explanation: He stood on trial because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead (Acts 23:6).

questions.prompt: What did the Lord promise Paul at night?
choices: He must also testify in Rome
questions.explanation: Take courage! … you must also testify in Rome (Acts 23:11).

questions.prompt: Who warned of the plot to ambush Paul?
questions.explanation: The son of Paul’s sister heard of the plot and reported it (Acts 23:16–22).

questions.prompt: What topics made Felix afraid when Paul spoke?
choices: Righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come
questions.explanation: As Paul talked about righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come, Felix was afraid (Acts 24:25).

title: Appeal, Storm, and the Gospel Unhindered
lesson: Festus suggests a Jerusalem trial; Paul appeals to Caesar. Before Agrippa he recounts the heavenly vision: Jesus sent him to open eyes, turn people from darkness to light and from Satan to God. Festus calls him insane; Agrippa is almost persuaded. Paul wishes all might become as he is—except for the chains.

On the voyage to Italy a violent storm strips hope from the crew. Paul shares an angel’s assurance: he must stand before Caesar, and God has granted him all who sail with him. All 276 reach Malta safely. A viper does Paul no harm; he heals many on the island.

In Rome Paul lives under guard, explains the hope of Israel, and from morning till evening teaches Jesus from the Law and Prophets. For two years he welcomes all who come, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance. Acts ends with an open door.

featuredVerse.text: He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ—with all boldness and without hindrance!

questions.prompt: Why did Paul appeal to Caesar?
choices: He refused an unfair Jerusalem transfer and used his right
questions.explanation: Paul appealed to Caesar after Festus suggested a Jerusalem trial (Acts 25:9–12).

questions.prompt: Jesus sent Paul to turn people from:
choices: Darkness to light and Satan to God
questions.explanation: To open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan to God (Acts 26:18).

questions.prompt: During the storm, what assurance did Paul share?
choices: He must stand before Caesar and God granted him all aboard
questions.explanation: An angel said Paul must stand before Caesar, and God had given him all who sailed with him (Acts 27:23–24).

questions.prompt: How many people reached land safely?
questions.explanation: In all there were 276 on board; everyone reached land safely (Acts 27:37, 44).

questions.prompt: In Rome Paul said he was in chains because of:
questions.explanation: It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain (Acts 28:20).

questions.prompt: How does Acts describe Paul’s ministry in Rome at the end?
choices: Bold and unhindered proclamation of the kingdom
questions.explanation: He proclaimed the kingdom and taught about Jesus with all boldness and without hindrance (Acts 28:30–31).
